About: Three Speeds, One Gas

Source

Topic
Kinetic theory of gases — molecular speed distribution
Concept
A gas has no single speed: the most-probable, mean, and rms speeds are three different numbers whose ratios are the same for every gas at every temperature.

Where do the three markers sit relative to each other on the distribution?

"The" average speed of a gas molecule — as if a single number existed.

Guided Inquiry

1. Predict — where do the three markers sit?

Imagine drawing three vertical lines on the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve: the most probable speed vp, the mean ⟨v⟩, and the root-mean-square vrms. Which picture is right?

2. Observe — let the histogram build

Press Play. Each molecule contributes its speed to the histogram every so often, so the bars grow ragged first and then settle onto the smooth Maxwell–Boltzmann curve. Watch the three markers on the histogram — they never move onto each other.

Read the ratio vrms/vp in the sidebar. Keep an eye on it while it fills in.

3. Predict — quadruple the temperature

You are about to drag T from 300 K to 1200 K. What happens to the three speeds and to the gaps between the markers?

4. Observe — T = 1200 K

Watch: T just quadrupled, and every one of the three markers doubled. The whole distribution has widened and flattened, but the ratio vrms/vp in the sidebar has NOT changed.

Now try helium instead of nitrogen — same story. Any gas, any temperature: the ratio is fixed at √(3/2) ≈ 1.2247.

5. The one thing to notice

A gas has no single speed. There are three standard ones — vp, ⟨v⟩, vrms — differing by about 22% end to end. Their ratios are fixed pure numbers, independent of gas and temperature:

vp : ⟨v⟩ : vrms = √2 : √(8/π) : √3
            = 1 : 1.128 : 1.225

Change T or M and every speed scales as √(T/M) together — the three markers move as a rigid unit.

01

At a glance

A box of gas molecules, each moving at its own speed, feeds a live histogram of those speeds. The sim asks what "the speed of a gas molecule" can mean when the molecules do not agree, and lets you compare three standard answers.

What you'll learn

  • What the most probable, mean and rms speeds each measure, and how they are defined.
  • How each of them depends on the temperature T and on the molar mass M of the gas.
  • How the three speeds are related to one another, and why that relation matters.
The sim keeps a box of moving molecules and a histogram that collects their speeds.

What's on screen

  • Molecules in a box (left): each dot is coloured by its speed, from blue (slow) to red (fast).
  • Speed distribution (right): teal bars from the molecules' speeds, and a smooth teal curve for the theory.
  • Three dashed markers on the histogram, one for each standard speed, each labelled with its value.
  • The three speeds panel in the sidebar, with the ratio of two of them.
See itRun nitrogen at 300 K. Watch for: coloured molecules moving in the box, and teal bars building up on the histogram.

03

Three standard speeds come from three different averages

The molecules of a gas have a whole spread of speeds, described by the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve f(v). No single number is "the speed", so physics uses three standard ones.

  • vp, the most probable speed. The speed at the peak of f(v): more molecules lie in a narrow band around it than around any other speed.
  • ⟨v⟩, the mean speed. Add up every molecule's speed and divide by the number of molecules.
  • vrms, the root-mean-square speed. Square every speed, average the squares, then take the square root.

The rms speed is the one tied to energy: the average of ½mv² over the molecules is ½m·vrms², where m is the mass of one molecule.

See itLook at the three markers on the histogram. Watch for: three dashed lines, amber, green and pink, each labelled with its own value in m/s.
04

The three speeds differ by fixed factors

With R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and M in kg/mol, integrating over f(v) gives

vp = √(2RT/M) · ⟨v⟩ = √(8RT/πM) · vrms = √(3RT/M)
The same RT/M sits under each root. Only the number in front differs.

The numbers are √2 = 1.414, √(8/π) = 1.596 and √3 = 1.732, so vp < ⟨v⟩ < vrms in every gas at every temperature. Dividing by √2 gives the ratios 1 : 1.128 : 1.225, and vrms/vp = √(3/2) = 1.2247.

The order has a cause. The curve has a long tail towards high speeds. The tail pulls the mean above the peak, and squaring before averaging pulls vrms up even more. For nitrogen at 300 K the sim gives 422.0, 476.2 and 516.8 m/s.

See itRead the three speeds and the ratio for nitrogen at 300 K. Watch for: the panel reading 422.0, 476.2 and 516.8 m/s, and the ratio box reading 1.2247.
05

Raising T scales every speed by the same factor

At a fixed gas, all three speeds are proportional to √T. Quadrupling T doubles every one of them, and the ratios between them do not change.

Nitrogenvp⟨v⟩vrms
300 K422.0 m/s476.2 m/s516.8 m/s
1200 K844.0 m/s952.3 m/s1033.7 m/s

The reason is energy: the average translational kinetic energy per molecule is proportional to T, and energy goes as speed squared. The whole curve also moves right and flattens. The area under f(v) stays 1, so when vp doubles, the peak height falls to half.

See itTake nitrogen from 300 K to 1200 K. Watch for: all three markers moving to twice their old values, the curve flatter and wider, and the ratio box still reading 1.2247.
06

At the same T a lighter gas is faster

At a fixed temperature, all three speeds are proportional to 1/√M. Every gas has the same average translational kinetic energy per molecule, (3/2)kT, so a molecule that is lighter must move faster to carry it.

  • Helium (4.00 g/mol) against nitrogen (28.0 g/mol): the speeds are in the ratio √(28.014/4.003) = 2.645.
  • At 300 K, vrms is 1367.2 m/s for helium, 516.8 m/s for nitrogen and 412.3 m/s for CO₂ (44.0 g/mol).
  • The ratios 1 : 1.128 : 1.225 are the same for every gas, because M cancels when the speeds are divided.

Temperature and mass appear only as the combination T/M. Warming a gas and swapping in a lighter gas both move the three markers together.

See itSwitch the gas from nitrogen to helium at 300 K. Watch for: the three speeds jumping to 1116.3, 1259.7 and 1367.2 m/s, and the ratio box still reading 1.2247.
07

The sim's histogram is a sample of 260 molecules

When a run starts, each of the 260 molecules is given a speed drawn from the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution for the current T and M. It keeps that speed for the whole run, bouncing off the walls. The box is drawn flat, but the speeds are three-dimensional speeds.

Every 0.05 s of sim time, the histogram adds all 260 speeds to its bars, scaled so that the total area is 1. The bars therefore trace the shape of the curve but scatter a little around it, because 260 molecules are a small sample. The markers come from the formulas, so they sit exactly at the values in the panel, while the sample's own mean and rms can differ from them slightly.

A real gas has about 10²² molecules in a litre, and collisions reshuffle their speeds many billions of times a second. The distribution stays the same while individual molecules change speed constantly.

See itLet nitrogen at 300 K run for a few seconds. Watch for: the teal bars rising and settling near the smooth curve, with a few bars sitting a little above or below it.
08

Where it matters

  • Effusion. A gas leaks through a tiny hole at a rate proportional to its mean speed, so proportional to 1/√M (Graham's law). Helium escapes about 2.6 times faster than nitrogen at the same temperature.
  • Light gases in the atmosphere. Escape from Earth needs about 11.2 km/s, far above vrms of helium at 300 K (1.4 km/s). Only the few molecules in the high-speed tail of the hot upper atmosphere get away, which is why light gases leak off over geological time.
  • Sound. Sound in a gas travels at √(γRT/M), which has the same √(T/M) dependence. In nitrogen at 300 K that is about 353 m/s, below vrms = 517 m/s.
  • Reaction rates. A reaction needs molecules with enough energy, which come from the tail of the distribution. A small rise in T adds many more molecules to the tail.
09

Summary

In one line. A gas has a whole spread of molecular speeds, so physics uses several standard speeds, each a different average of that spread.

Key points

  • vp = √(2RT/M), ⟨v⟩ = √(8RT/πM) and vrms = √(3RT/M), in the ratio 1 : 1.128 : 1.225.
  • All three scale as √(T/M): they double when T is quadrupled and fall as the gas gets heavier.
  • The sim's histogram samples 260 molecules; the markers come from the formulas.

Common mix-ups

  • "The average speed is the speed most molecules have." The mean is 12.8% above the most probable speed. They are different numbers.
  • "At four times the temperature, molecules move four times as fast." Speed goes as √T, so it only doubles. The average kinetic energy is what quadruples.
  • "A heavier gas at the same temperature has more translational kinetic energy per molecule." The average is (3/2)kT for every gas. Heavier molecules carry it by moving more slowly.

Things to try on your own

  • Read vrms for nitrogen at 77 K and at 1500 K, and check that their ratio equals √(1500/77) = 4.41.
  • Choose CO₂ and find the temperature at which its vrms matches nitrogen's at 300 K.
  • Pick three different pairs of T and gas, and divide ⟨v⟩ by vp each time.
